questions.q: In the Harborline case study, why was Service Cloud's Case object rejected as the basis for the Maintenance Request entity?
options: Because Case objects cannot be customized with any new fields
Because Service Cloud was not licensed by Harborline at all
Because its lifecycle and audience (customer-facing support) didn't match the internal equipment-maintenance workflow closely enough to force the fit
Because Case cannot have a master-detail relationship to any custom object
questions.explain: The case study explicitly reasons through cloud/feature fit (Lesson 7) and rejects Case because its support-oriented lifecycle and audience don't match the internal maintenance workflow, rather than forcing a standard object to fit.

questions.q: Why did the case study design a master-detail relationship from Maintenance Request to Equipment, rather than a lookup?
options: Because a Maintenance Request has no independent meaning without its Equipment -- the lifecycle reasoning from Lesson 16 pointed to master-detail
Because master-detail is always required for any custom object relationship
Because lookup relationships cannot be created between two custom objects
Because master-detail relationships are faster to query in every case
questions.explain: This follows Lesson 16's lifecycle reasoning directly: a Request only makes sense in the context of its Equipment, which is exactly the signal for master-detail rather than lookup.

questions.q: Why did the case study's automation design stay entirely declarative, with no Apex introduced?
options: Because Apex is technically impossible to use on the core Salesforce Platform
Because Flow cannot create related records under any circumstances
Because the company had no custom objects in its data model
Because, given the eight-week timeline and part-time-admin maintenance constraint, the complexity factors from Lesson 5 didn't clear the bar for programmatic logic
questions.explain: The case study explicitly ties the declarative-only automation decision back to Lesson 5's factors, given the project's realistic constraints (timeline, maintenance capacity) and the actual complexity of the automation needed.

questions.q: What was the deliberate technical-debt decision documented in the Harborline case study, per this lesson?
options: Skipping requirements intake entirely to save time
Descoping the full manager-visibility dashboard to a simple list view for launch, with a documented note that a proper dashboard is planned for a follow-up phase
Building the application directly on the Case object despite the mismatch
Leaving the data model entirely undocumented
questions.explain: The case study explicitly names the dashboard descoping as a deliberate, documented debt decision -- consistent with Lesson 11's deliberate-vs-reckless debt distinction -- rather than a silently dropped requirement.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what would a less disciplined team have gotten backwards if they prioritized building the full manager dashboard over mobile-first design for the technician's submission screen?
options: Nothing -- both choices would have had identical real-world impact
Manager dashboards are always more technically complex than mobile screens, so this would be the correct priority

They would have deprioritized the non-functional requirement (mobile field submission under poor connectivity) most likely to cause real daily friction, in favor of a less urgent desktop-facing feature
Mobile-first design is only relevant for Experience Cloud sites, not internal field use
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls this out as 'exactly backwards' -- the technician's poor-connectivity mobile submission screen was the non-functional requirement most likely to cause real daily friction, making it the wrong thing to deprioritize.
